newsitem.title: COMOROS: Airline coffin bobs in sea by plush Comoro hotel.
newsitem.headline: Airline coffin bobs in sea by plush Comoro hotel.

text.p: Divers at a luxury Comoro Islands resort on Sunday recalled the horror of seeing an Ethiopian Airlines jet crash into the coral reef just metres (yards) away from them.

"I heard the most violent crashing noise as the jet crunched into the coral," said Alex Coinchelin, a young French diving instructor who had been just off the beach down in the turquoise waters of the Indian Ocean with a group of 10 tourists.
"In the water you don't know where the noise is coming from, it's all around. I rushed to the surface. I could not believe it."
Just 100 metres away the jet, which had run out of fuel after being hijacked in Ethiopia on Saturday, had rammed into the sea and broken open into three or four pieces.
Coinchelin, and colleagues who had been sitting out at sea in a boat near where the plane hit the water said they started immediately to rescue people from the wreckage.
Some of the 170-plus people on board were trapped in their seats above the water -- others below.

"I didn't stop to think about it all at the time, you just do it straight away. We cut seatbelts and pulled people out. But it was hard to look -- some had smashed heads and all their eyes were open," he said.
"I couldn't believe I was suddenly there among people swimming, bleeding, crying in the water. Many were dead in their seats, their seatbelts still fastened."

Rescue operations continued on Sunday to try to retrieve 50 to 70 bodies, many trapped in the twisted fuselage that bobbed up and down in the water, partly submerged and drifting ever closer to shore.
Bodies retrieved on Sunday had been taken to the main town, with survivors taken to the hospital there or flown out to the nearby French island of Reunion or to Nairobi.
The scene at the Le Galawa Beach hotel, 40km (25 milies) from the island capital Moroni, was bizarre as mainly French and South Africans continued their holidays -- in a subdued way.
Boards posted Monday's diving trips and excursions around the volcanic island of banana and coconut groves, east of Mozambique.

Some tourists lounging on deck chairs read magazines and tanned themselves by the hotel pool, their backs turned to the sea where, just 400 metres (486 yards) behind them, black dinghies full of French military divers circled the white wreckage.

Others, along with hundreds of local villagers kept at a distance, sat on the white-sand, palm-fringed beach, staring at the fuselage and the green tail of the Boeing 767, jutting out of the waters where it crashed.
"It was hideous down there. Bodies everywhere, including a girl whose hair waved around in the water," said Coinchelin, 26.
The Dijon man, working the island for the holiday season, said he dived for about 90 minutes, as long as his oxygen tank lasted, bringing out first some survivors then only the dead.
